# 1 Samuel Chapter 24 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 164v–165r | **Source Image:** 1SA_024_page_001.jpg, 1SA_024_page_002.jpg

---

**1** After Saul returned from fighting the Philistines, he was told, "David is in the Wilderness of En-gedi."

**2** So Saul took three thousand of Israel's best soldiers and went to search for David and his men among the Crags of the Wild Goats.

**3** He came to the sheep pens along the road, where there was a cave. Saul went inside to relieve himself — while David and his men were sitting deep in the back of that very cave.

**4** David's men whispered, "This is the day the LORD told you about: 'I will hand your enemy over to you, and you may do with him as you see fit.'" David crept forward and secretly cut off a corner of Saul's robe.

**5** Immediately afterward, David's conscience stung him for cutting even that piece of Saul's robe.

**6** He told his men, "The LORD forbid that I should do such a thing to my master — the LORD's anointed. I will not raise my hand against him, for he is the LORD's anointed."

**7** With these words David restrained his men and did not let them attack Saul. Then Saul left the cave and went on his way.

**8** After that, David came out of the cave and called after him, "My lord the king!" When Saul looked back, David bowed face down to the ground in homage.

**9** David said to Saul, "Why do you listen to people who say, 'David is out to harm you'?

**10** This very day you can see with your own eyes that the LORD put you in my power in that cave. I was urged to kill you, but I spared you. I said, 'I will not raise my hand against my master, because he is the LORD's anointed.'

**11** Look, my father — look at this piece of your robe in my hand! I cut the corner of your robe and did not kill you. Surely you can see that I have no intention of harming you or rebelling against you. I have not wronged you, yet you are hunting me down to take my life.

**12** Let the LORD judge between us. Let the LORD avenge the wrongs done to me — but my hand will never touch you.

**13** As the old proverb says, 'From the wicked comes wickedness' — but my hand will never touch you.

**14** Look at what the king of Israel has come out to pursue! A dead dog! A single flea!

**15** May the LORD be the judge between us. May he consider my case, plead my cause, and deliver me from your hand."

**16** When David finished speaking, Saul said, "Is that your voice, my son David?" And Saul broke down and wept.

**17** He said to David, "You are more righteous than I am. You have repaid me with good, while I have repaid you with evil.

**18** You have proven today how well you have treated me — the LORD delivered me into your hands, and you did not kill me.

**19** What man, finding his enemy, would let him walk away unharmed? May the LORD reward you richly for what you have done for me today.

**20** Now I know for certain that you will be king and that the kingdom of Israel will be established in your hands.

**21** Swear to me now by the LORD that you will not cut off my descendants after me and that you will not wipe out my name from my father's family."

**22** David gave Saul his oath. Then Saul went home, and David and his men went back up to the stronghold.

---

## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

The cave at En-gedi is one of the great dramatic scenes of the Hebrew Bible — a moment of maximum temptation framed as divine gift. David's men interpret the encounter theologically ("This is the day the LORD told you about"), but David reads the moment differently. The cutting of the *kanaf* (corner/hem) of Saul's robe is no mere prank; the robe's hem symbolized royal authority and dignity in the ancient Near East. David has symbolically seized the kingship — and is immediately horrified at himself.

The phrase in v. 5, *vayakh lev-David oto* ("his heart struck him"), describes what we might call a pang of conscience. This interior moral reflex — guilt not for violence committed but for a symbolic violation of the LORD's anointed — is central to David's characterization. He holds himself to a standard his men do not share.

David's speech (vv. 9-15) is a masterpiece of rhetoric: evidence (the robe corner), principle (the anointed cannot be touched), proverb (wickedness comes from the wicked), self-deprecation (dead dog, flea), and appeal to divine judgment. The progression moves from proof to plea, from human restraint to divine adjudication.

Saul's weeping in v. 16 and his confession in v. 17 (*tsaddiq attah mimmeni*, "you are more righteous than I") represent a moment of devastating lucidity. He sees himself clearly — and he knows the kingdom is already David's. His request to preserve his descendants (v. 21) is the plea of a man who has seen his own dynasty's end.

— PNEUMA
